claim: The survey collected 7,603 responses from postdocs based at 351 US academic and non-academic institutions in 2016.
source: Here we present comprehensive survey results from 7,603 postdocs based at 351 US academic and non-academic (e.g. hospital, industry and government lab) institutions in 2016.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of respondents and institutions in the abstract and results sections.

claim: Academic research positions remain the predominant career choice among postdocs.
source: Academic research positions remain the predominant career choice, although women and US citizens are less likely than their male and non-US citizen counterparts to choose academic research positions.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by survey data presented in the results.

claim: Women are less likely than men to choose academic research positions.
source: Academic research positions remain the predominant career choice, although women and US citizens are less likely than their male and non-US citizen counterparts to choose academic research positions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this gender difference, supported by statistical analysis in the results.

claim: US citizens are less likely than non-US citizens to choose academic research positions.
source: Academic research positions remain the predominant career choice, although women and US citizens are less likely than their male and non-US citizen counterparts to choose academic research positions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this citizenship-based difference, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Receiving mentorship training has a significant positive effect on postdoc satisfaction with mentorship.
source: Receiving mentorship training has a significant positive effect on postdoc satisfaction with mentorship.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by nominal logistic regression analysis in the results.

claim: Quality of and satisfaction with postdoc mentorship appear to heavily influence career choice.
source: Quality of and satisfaction with postdoc mentorship also appear to heavily influence career choice.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by multivariate analysis in the results section.

claim: Tenure-track faculty positions are estimated to represent approximately 15% of postdoc career outcomes.
source: Tenure-track faculty positions, however, are now estimated to represent a small percentage of postdoc career outcomes (~15%) (Larson et al., 2014; National Academy of Sciences, 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites two sources for this estimate.

claim: The postdoctoral experience has not been comprehensively surveyed nationally in over a decade prior to this study.
source: Possibly for these very reasons, the postdoctoral experience has not been comprehensively surveyed nationally in over a decade, following the Sigma Xi 'Doctors without orders' survey report in 2005, which was based on postdoc respondents from 46 participating institutions (Davis, 2005).
evidence: The introduction states this gap in data collection with citation to the previous survey.

claim: The Sigma Xi 'Doctors without orders' survey in 2005 was based on postdoc respondents from 46 participating institutions.
source: Possibly for these very reasons, the postdoctoral experience has not been comprehensively surveyed nationally in over a decade, following the Sigma Xi 'Doctors without orders' survey report in 2005, which was based on postdoc respondents from 46 participating institutions (Davis, 2005).

evidence: The results section provides specific citizenship status percentages by gender with statistical test results.

source: In addition, a small but significantly higher proportion of male postdocs were married/partnered (Male: 68.3%, Female: 63.2%, n = 7,538, χ2 = 21.693, p < 0.0001) and/or have children (Male: 31.0%, Female: 22.3%, n = 7,532, χ2 = 71.561, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The results section provides specific percentages by gender with statistical test results.

claim: A small but significantly higher proportion of male postdocs have children (Male: 31.0%, Female: 22.3%).

evidence: The results section provides specific percentages by gender with statistical test results.

claim: The gender disparity in pay was present even after controlling for age, years since graduation, race/ethnicity, satisfaction with mentorship, Carnegie classification of institution, public or private control of institution, marital status, and parental status.
source: The gender disparity in pay was present even after male and female postdocs were matched in age, years since graduation, self-identification as white/Caucasian or other, satisfaction with mentorship, Carnegie classification of institution, public or private control of institution, whether married/partnered, or having children (nominal logistic regression model, gender effect test n = 7,280, χ2 = 51.330, p < 0.0001; Supplementary file 1 (Table S4)).
evidence: The results section describes the nominal logistic regression model controlling for multiple factors.

claim: Female postdocs earned less than male postdocs, regardless of type of institution, marital status, parental status, or majority/minority status.
source: In other words, female postdocs earned less than male postdocs, regardless of type of institution, marital status, parental status, or majority/minority status.
evidence: The results section summarizes the findings from the regression model.

claim: The gender wage gap increased with postdoc age but not with partnership status.
source: This gender wage gap increased with postdoc age but not with partnership status, partially supporting previous analyses of the STEM gender wage gap (Association of American University Professors, 2006; Athanasiadou et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section states this finding with citations to previous work.

claim: Postdocs in Engineering, Environmental Sciences, the Physical Sciences, and the Social Sciences earn significantly more money than postdocs in the Life Sciences, Humanities, Medicine, or Psychology.
source: Primary field of study was excluded from this analysis because field has such a large effect on salary, overshadowing most other factors, with postdocs in Engineering, Environmental Sciences, the Physical Sciences, and the Social Sciences earning significantly more money than postdocs in the Life Sciences, Humanities, Medicine, or Psychology (n = 7,542, 750.452, p < 0.0001; Supplementary file 1 (Table S5)).
evidence: The results section provides this field-based salary comparison with statistical test results.

claim: 58% of postdocs at national government laboratories report earning more than $55,000 a year.
source: Carnegie classification also had a large effect on salary (Supplementary file 1 (Table S4)), as 58% of the postdocs at national government laboratories report earning more than $55,000 a year, while only 8% of postdocs at R1 institutions report earning more than $55,000 a year.
evidence: The results section provides this salary comparison by institution type.

claim: Only 8% of postdocs at R1 institutions report earning more than $55,000 a year.
source: Carnegie classification also had a large effect on salary (Supplementary file 1 (Table S4)), as 58% of the postdocs at national government laboratories report earning more than $55,000 a year, while only 8% of postdocs at R1 institutions report earning more than $55,000 a year.
evidence: The results section provides this salary comparison by institution type.

claim: Male postdocs were more likely than women to be in the primary fields of Engineering or Physical Sciences.
source: Male postdocs were more likely than women to be in the primary fields of Engineering (n = 620, χ2 = 76.652, p < 0.0001) or Physical Sciences (n = 846, χ2 = 77.466, p < 0.0001), two fields which have historically higher salaries (Buffington et al., 2016).
evidence: The results section provides this field distribution by gender with statistical test results and citation.

source: Male postdocs were more likely than women to be in the primary fields of Engineering (n = 620, χ2 = 76.652, p < 0.0001) or Physical Sciences (n = 846, χ2 = 77.466, p < 0.0001), two fields which have historically higher salaries (Buffington et al., 2016).
evidence: The results section cites Buffington et al. for this historical salary information.

source: Interestingly, female postdocs trended towards being paid less than men in all fields except the Physical Sciences, where women trended towards being paid slightly more than men (Supplementary file 1 (Table S5)).
evidence: The results section describes this field-specific gender pay pattern with reference to supplementary data.

source: Most postdocs reported salaries in the range of $39,000–$55,000 (median $43,750, mean $46,988, n = 7,551).

source: Although salaries in high cost of living (COL) urban areas tend to be higher than average (Supplementary file 1 (Table S6)), when adjusted to publicly available COL data, postdocs in large metropolitan areas earn significantly less money than postdocs in college towns or rural settings (average salary when adjusted for cost of living, metropolitan: $38,045.60; non-metropolitan: $44,714.40; n = 7,551, F-ratio:12.614, p = 0.0002; Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1 (Table S6)).
evidence: The results section provides this cost-of-living adjusted salary comparison with statistical test results.

claim: The majority of postdocs selected research-focused academic careers as their primary long-term career plan (57.7%), with industry research a distant second (17.8%).
source: The majority of postdocs selected research-focused academic careers as their primary long-term career plan (57.7%), with industry research a distant second (17.8%; Figure 1J; Supplementary file 1 (Table S2)).
evidence: The results section provides these specific career choice percentages with reference to figure and supplementary data.

claim: A nominal logistic regression model identified 14 significant factors influencing postdoc career plan.
source: To assess which factors were most influential for determining postdoc career plan in our dataset (categorized in this survey as: academia, primarily research based; academia, primarily teaching based; industry; government/non-profit; other) we conducted a nominal logistic regression model with 26 factors concerning topics considered to be important for postdoc success and career choice (Supplementary file 1 (Table S7)), which include demographics, training, productivity and mentor support matrices. The 14 significant factors in the model were (in order of effect size): 1) whether postdoc career plans had changed; 2) whether the postdoc received training in pedagogy; 3) feelings of career preparedness; 4) perceived support of career plan from mentors; 5) primary field of study; 6) residency status in the US; 7) intensity of job search; 8) postdoc gender; 9) number of first, last, or corresponding author publications; 10) number of conferences attended in the past year; 11) hours worked per week; 12) total number of publications while a postdoc; 13) mentor rank; and 14) desire to pursue a career in the US (Table 1).
evidence: The results section describes the regression model and lists all 14 significant factors.

claim: Perceived mentor support, number of postdoc publications, hours worked per week, conferences attended, and postdoc feelings of career preparedness were all positively correlated with a choice to pursue a research-focused academic career.
source: Perceived mentor support, number of postdoc publications, hours worked per week, conferences attended, and postdoc feelings of career preparedness were all positively correlated with a choice to pursue a research-focused academic career (Figure 3A,B,D–F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The results section states these positive correlations with reference to figures.

claim: Male postdocs were more interested in academic research positions than female postdocs.
source: Male postdocs, and postdocs who were not US citizens, were more interested in academic research positions (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The results section states this gender difference with reference to figure.

claim: Postdocs who were not US citizens were more interested in academic research positions.
source: Male postdocs, and postdocs who were not US citizens, were more interested in academic research positions (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The results section states this citizenship-based difference with reference to figure.

claim: Postdocs with mentors outside of the professoriate were more likely to prefer government/non-profit positions.
source: In contrast, postdocs with mentors outside of the professoriate were more likely to prefer government/non-profit positions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section states this mentor-type effect with reference to figure.

claim: Postdocs with non-academic mentors changed their career plans at the same rate as those with academic mentors.
source: Whether this is a cause or effect relationship is not clear from our study, though we did find that postdocs with non-academic mentors changed their career plans at the same rate as those with academic mentors (n = 7,361, χ2 = 6.860, p = 0.077).
evidence: The results section provides this finding with statistical test results.

claim: Postdocs actively searching for permanent positions were less interested in academic research than postdocs not yet on the job market.
source: In addition, postdocs actively searching for permanent positions were less interested in academic research than postdocs not yet on the job market (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and were more likely to have changed their career plans (n = 7,565, χ2 = 224.633, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The results section states this job search effect with reference to figure and statistical test results.

claim: Postdocs actively searching for permanent positions were more likely to have changed their career plans.
source: In addition, postdocs actively searching for permanent positions were less interested in academic research than postdocs not yet on the job market (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and were more likely to have changed their career plans (n = 7,565, χ2 = 224.633, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The results section provides this finding with statistical test results.

claim: Individual career choice is influenced by changing job attribute preferences and self-awareness.
source: These results complement recent studies suggesting that individual career choice is influenced by changing job attribute preferences and self-awareness (Buffington et al., 2016), and that academic success is influenced by mentorship during the postdoctoral period (Lienard et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section cites Buffington et al. for this career choice mechanism.

claim: Academic success is influenced by mentorship during the postdoctoral period.
source: These results complement recent studies suggesting that individual career choice is influenced by changing job attribute preferences and self-awareness (Buffington et al., 2016), and that academic success is influenced by mentorship during the postdoctoral period (Lienard et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section cites Lienard et al. for this mentorship effect.

claim: Sixty percent of respondents were either satisfied or very satisfied with the mentorship they receive.
source: Sixty percent of respondents were either satisfied or very satisfied with the mentorship they receive, with similar responses from both genders (Figure 1I).
evidence: The results section provides this satisfaction percentage with reference to figure.

claim: Both genders reported similar levels of satisfaction with mentorship.
source: Sixty percent of respondents were either satisfied or very satisfied with the mentorship they receive, with similar responses from both genders (Figure 1I).
evidence: The results section states this lack of gender difference with reference to figure.

claim: A nominal logistic regression model identified eight significant factors influencing satisfaction with postdoc mentor.
source: To assess which factors were most influential for determining satisfaction with their postdoc mentor, we conducted a nominal logistic regression model with the same 26 factors included in the model for postdoc career choice (though excluding satisfaction with mentorship as a factor, and replacing it with postdoc long-term career plan; Supplementary file 1 (Table S7)). The eight significant factors in the model (in order of effect size) were: 1) feelings of career preparedness; 2) perceived support of career plan from mentors; 3) frequency of project meetings with mentor; 4) intensity of job search; 5) whether the postdoc received training in mentorship; 6) primary field of study; 7) perception of job market; and 8) academic rank of mentor (Table 2).
evidence: The results section describes the regression model and lists all eight significant factors.

claim: Factors influencing satisfaction with mentor were more important than number of postdoc publications, whether a postdoc had changed career plans, postdoc or mentor gender, residency status, or postdoc training in either grant writing or pedagogy.
source: These factors were more important than number of postdoc publications, whether a postdoc had changed career plans, postdoc or mentor gender, residency status, or postdoc training in either grant writing or pedagogy.
evidence: The results section states which factors were not significant in the model.

claim: Perceived mentor support had a positive effect on how satisfied a postdoc is with their mentor.
source: Perceived mentor support had a positive effect on how satisfied a postdoc is with their mentor, as did frequency of mentor meetings, perception of preparedness for desired future career, and perception of job market (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The results section states this positive effect with reference to figure.

claim: Frequency of mentor meetings had a positive effect on how satisfied a postdoc is with their mentor.
source: Perceived mentor support had a positive effect on how satisfied a postdoc is with their mentor, as did frequency of mentor meetings, perception of preparedness for desired future career, and perception of job market (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The results section states this positive effect with reference to figure.

claim: Perception of preparedness for desired future career had a positive effect on how satisfied a postdoc is with their mentor.
source: Perceived mentor support had a positive effect on how satisfied a postdoc is with their mentor, as did frequency of mentor meetings, perception of preparedness for desired future career, and perception of job market (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The results section states this positive effect with reference to figure.

claim: Perception of job market had a positive effect on how satisfied a postdoc is with their mentor.
source: Perceived mentor support had a positive effect on how satisfied a postdoc is with their mentor, as did frequency of mentor meetings, perception of preparedness for desired future career, and perception of job market (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The results section states this positive effect with reference to figure.

claim: Postdocs who received training in mentorship were more satisfied with the mentorship they received than postdocs who did not receive training in mentorship.
source: Postdocs who received training in mentorship were more satisfied with the mentorship they received than postdocs who did not receive training in mentorship (Figure 4E).
evidence: The results section states this effect with reference to figure.

claim: Only 26% of postdocs reported that they have received mentorship training.
source: We found this to be particularly noteworthy, as mentorship training is not a common part of the postdoctoral experience, with only 26% of postdocs reporting that they have received such training.
evidence: The results section provides this percentage of postdocs receiving mentorship training.

claim: High satisfaction with mentorship and perceived support correlated with increased interest in an academic research focused career in a previous postdoc cohort study.
source: Previous research on a postdoc cohort showed that high satisfaction with mentorship and perceived support correlated with increased interest in an academic research focused career (Scaffidi and Berman, 2011).
evidence: The results section cites Scaffidi and Berman for this previous finding.

claim: Group career coaching was found to increase both perceived 'achievability' and 'desirability' of academic careers in an under-represented minority student group.
source: In addition, in a randomized, controlled study, a different type of mentoring, 'group career coaching,' where a career coach works with small groups of graduate students to provide support and promote career progress, was found to increase both perceived 'achievability' and 'desirability' of academic careers in an under-represented minority student group (Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: The results section cites Williams et al. for this career coaching intervention finding.

claim: In a longitudinal study of PhD students interested in academic careers, their perceived ability, or self-efficacy, was a strong indicator of retaining interest in a faculty career.
source: Thirdly, in a longitudinal study of PhD students interested in academic careers, their perceived ability, or self-efficacy, was a strong indicator of retaining interest in a faculty career (Roach and Sauermann, 2017).
evidence: The results section cites Roach and Sauermann for this self-efficacy finding.

claim: Provision of research mentor training improves the success of researchers-in-training at all levels.
source: Other studies suggest that in addition to structured oversight and professional development (Davis, 2009), provision of research mentor training improves the success of researchers-in-training at all levels (Fleming et al., 2012).
evidence: The results section cites Fleming et al. for this mentor training effect.

claim: Increasing a graduate student or postdoc's self confidence and self-efficacy increases interest in an academic faculty career.
source: These studies strongly suggest that increasing a graduate student or postdoc's self confidence and self-efficacy increases interest in an academic faculty career.
evidence: The results section infers this conclusion from the cited studies.

claim: Self-efficacy is directly impacted by the primary mentor.
source: Self-efficacy is directly impacted by the primary mentor and may explain the correlation between perceived support from their mentor and a postdoc's interest in a faculty career seen here and elsewhere (Scaffidi and Berman, 2011).
evidence: The results section infers this mechanism with citation to supporting work.

claim: There is no significant correlation between gender and satisfaction with mentor.
source: While our data do not show a significant correlation between gender and satisfaction with their mentor, they do suggest that an increase in mentor support and mentorship training will increase a postdoc's interest in academic jobs.
evidence: The results section states this lack of gender effect on mentor satisfaction.

claim: An increase in mentor support and mentorship training will increase a postdoc's interest in academic jobs.
source: While our data do not show a significant correlation between gender and satisfaction with their mentor, they do suggest that an increase in mentor support and mentorship training will increase a postdoc's interest in academic jobs.
